input.hypothesis: Democrats take the House in the 2026 midterms

nodes.statement: By May 2026, the 2026 House midterm environment remains historically unfavorable to the president's party (generic ballot within 3 points of even or worse for GOP).
nodes.resolution: Resolvable via RealClearPolitics/538 generic-ballot averages and special-election results through 2026-05-15.
nodes.rationale: Off-year elections since WWII have almost always cost the president's party House seats; 2025 specials (VA, NJ, IA) showed elevated Democratic overperformance. A 90-day horizon only updates the environment, not the election itself.
assumptions: No major third-party or redistricting shock before May 2026
Generic ballot remains a valid predictor at this horizon
No recession-level economic shock in the window
nodes.marketQuery: Will Democrats win the House majority in the 2026 midterms?

nodes.name: Generic ballot (Dem lead, RCP average)
nodes.rationale: Democrats led recent 2025 polling averages by low single digits; off-year environments historically drift 1-2 points further against the incumbent party as the election nears.
assumptions: Polling averages are unbiased at this horizon
No major event shifts fundamentals >1 sigma
House effect roughly tracks generic ballot

nodes.name: Trump job approval (net)
nodes.rationale: Net approval in the negative single digits historically maps to meaningful House losses for the president's party; approval below -5 has preceded wave-level losses in 2018 analog.
assumptions: Approval is a leading indicator of midterm vote
No rally event in the 90-day window

nodes.statement: A federal government funding fight or shutdown in the window produces measurable blame attribution to Republicans (net approval drop of 2+ points).
nodes.resolution: Resolvable via funding deadlines, CBO/Congressional Record, and post-event approval polling through 2026-05-15.
nodes.rationale: Recurring funding deadlines create shutdown risk; 2013 and 2018-19 shutdowns showed modest incumbent-party approval costs, typically 1-3 points, fading within weeks.
assumptions: Funding deadline falls inside the window
No bipartisan deal removes the trigger
nodes.marketQuery: Will there be a US government shutdown before May 2026?

nodes.statement: Economic fundamentals (inflation near 3%, soft labor market) keep consumer sentiment depressed through May 2026.
nodes.resolution: Resolvable via CPI releases, unemployment rate, and University of Michigan sentiment through 2026-05-15.
nodes.rationale: Sentiment has remained historically depressed relative to hard data; inflation persistence and soft hiring typically weigh on incumbent-party midterm performance.
assumptions: No rapid disinflation or hiring boom
nodes.marketQuery: Will US CPI inflation exceed 3% year-over-year in April 2026?

nodes.statement: Democratic House candidates outraise Republican incumbents in Q1 2026 FEC filings in a majority of competitive districts.
nodes.resolution: Resolvable via FEC quarterly reports due April 15, 2026.
nodes.rationale: Out-party enthusiasm in hostile environments has produced fundraising edges in 2017 and 2021 cycles; Q1 filings are the first broad signal of candidate quality and energy.
assumptions: FEC filings are comparable across parties
nodes.marketQuery: Will Democrats outraise Republicans in Q1 2026 House competitive-district fundraising?

nodes.statement: Mid-cycle Republican-friendly redistricting (TX, MO, IN, and possible blue-state responses) nets the GOP 3-5 House seats before the election.
nodes.resolution: Resolvable via enacted state maps and court rulings through 2026-05-15.
nodes.rationale: Texas's 2025 mid-cycle map plus GOP pushes in Missouri/Indiana and Democratic counter-maps in CA/NY could shift the effective majority threshold by several seats.
nodes.marketQuery: Will new congressional maps net Republicans at least 3 additional House seats for 2026?

nodes.statement: Democrats overperform 2024 baseline by 5+ points in House specials and state-legislative specials held through May 2026.
nodes.resolution: Resolvable via special-election margins vs. partisan baselines (e.g., Daily Kos Elections) through 2026-05-15.
nodes.rationale: 2025 specials showed consistent double-digit Democratic overperformance; such signals historically precede favorable generic-ballot environments, though with diminishing magnitude.
assumptions: Specials are low-turnout and overstate general margins
nodes.marketQuery: Will Democrats overperform in upcoming 2026 House special elections?

nodes.statement: Democrats win a House majority in the November 2026 midterms (218+ seats).
nodes.resolution: Resolvable via AP/Dave Wasserman calls of all House races after 2026-11-03.
nodes.rationale: Combining a hostile incumbent-party environment, historical midterm seat losses (avg ~26 for presidents with sub-50% approval), and redistricting offsets yields a modest Democratic edge, not a wave.
assumptions: Generic ballot converts to seats near historical elasticity
No third-party collapse or turnout anomaly
nodes.marketQuery: Will Democrats win 218+ House seats in the 2026 midterms?

edges.mechanism: Hostile incumbent environment shows up as generic-ballot drift against GOP
assumptions: Polling averages incorporate specials and approval
Drift of 1-2 points per quarter typical

edges.mechanism: Presidential approval anchors nationalized House vote
Shutdown blame attribution depresses presidential and congressional approval
assumptions: Blame falls on GOP per 2013/2019 pattern

edges.mechanism: Depressed sentiment penalizes incumbent party on the ballot
Out-party fundraising edge signals enthusiasm reinforcing hostile environment
assumptions: Money predicts candidate quality and turnout

edges.mechanism: Special-election overperformance is a leading indicator of generic-ballot movement
Counter-force: GOP-friendly maps raise the seat threshold Democrats must clear
assumptions: 3-5 seat GOP gain from mid-cycle redistricting

edges.mechanism: Generic ballot converts to seats via historical elasticity (~1.5-2 points per 10 seats)
Historical midterm penalty: president's party loses seats when approval <50%
assumptions: 2026 GOP margin thin enough that typical loss flips majority

summary.headline: Democrats are modest favorites (~60-65%) to take the House in 2026, driven by the historical midterm penalty on the president's party, offset by mid-cycle redistricting gains for the GOP.
summary.mainUncertainty: Whether the generic ballot holds a 2-4 point Democratic edge through spring 2026, and how many seats mid-cycle redistricting nets the GOP.
followUps: Track Q1 2026 FEC filings for Democratic fundraising edge in competitive districts
Watch government funding deadlines for shutdown blame dynamics
Monitor special-election overperformance vs 2024 baselines through May 2026
Track litigation outcomes on TX/CA/NY congressional maps
